"title": "A schematic model of scattering in PT-symmetric Quantum Mechanics",
"authors": "Miloslav Znojil",
"field_subfield": "Theoretical physics: PT-symmetric quantum mechanics / one-dimensional scattering",
"type_of_paper": "Analytical/theoretical derivation with schematic numerical discretization",
"executive_summary": "This paper develops a schematic, exactly solvable model of one-dimensional scattering in PT-symmetric quantum mechanics, where the potential V(x) is complex but possesses combined parity-time symmetry. The author begins by recalling the standard treatment of stationary one-dimensional motion via the ordinary differential Schrödinger equation, which admits either bound-state solutions with ψ(±∞) = 0 or scattering solutions with incoming and outgoing plane-wave boundary conditions. The conventional approach specifies reflection and transmission coefficients B and C once the normalization A = 1 is imposed. The recent generalization to non-Hermitian but quasi-Hermitian Hamiltonians, characterized by PT-symmetry, is then invoked, with the key review by Carl Bender cited as the source of this development. The present work focuses on a very simple PT-symmetric scattering model in which the potential is written as V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x), with Z even and real, and Y odd and real. Rather than solving the differential equation directly, the author replaces it with its Runge-Kutta-discretized, difference-equation representation, a purely numerical recipe whose accuracy improves as the lattice step h tends to zero. Assuming the potential vanishes beyond a cutoff distance, the discrete Schrödinger equation reduces to a tridiagonal linear system, which can be solved either by a matching method or by a matrix-inversion method. The matrix-inversion approach reduces the problem to a two-dimensional matrix inversion, with all dynamical input encoded in two coefficients α and β that are rational functions of the coupling constants. The paper derives explicit formulae for the reflection and transmission coefficients and emphasizes that the only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter, namely the introduction of the imaginary part Y(x). The author illustrates the growing algebraic complexity of the determinant and numerator at increasing cutoff dimensions M = 2, 3, 4, noting that symbolic manipulation on a computer becomes necessary at M ≥ 4. The discussion situates the work within the broader PT-symmetry literature, highlighting the manifest asymmetry between in and out states, and concludes that the formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering is established, with the merit of the discrete model left for future study.",

summary.title: A schematic model of scattering in PT-symmetric Quantum Mechanics
summary.field_subfield: Theoretical physics: PT-symmetric quantum mechanics / one-dimensional scattering
summary.type_of_paper: Analytical/theoretical derivation with schematic numerical discretization
summary.executive_summary: This paper develops a schematic, exactly solvable model of one-dimensional scattering in PT-symmetric quantum mechanics, where the potential V(x) is complex but possesses combined parity-time symmetry. The author begins by recalling the standard treatment of stationary one-dimensional motion via the ordinary differential Schrödinger equation, which admits either bound-state solutions with ψ(±∞) = 0 or scattering solutions with incoming and outgoing plane-wave boundary conditions. The conventional approach specifies reflection and transmission coefficients B and C once the normalization A = 1 is imposed. The recent generalization to non-Hermitian but quasi-Hermitian Hamiltonians, characterized by PT-symmetry, is then invoked, with the key review by Carl Bender cited as the source of this development. The present work focuses on a very simple PT-symmetric scattering model in which the potential is written as V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x), with Z even and real, and Y odd and real. Rather than solving the differential equation directly, the author replaces it with its Runge-Kutta-discretized, difference-equation representation, a purely numerical recipe whose accuracy improves as the lattice step h tends to zero. Assuming the potential vanishes beyond a cutoff distance, the discrete Schrödinger equation reduces to a tridiagonal linear system, which can be solved either by a matching method or by a matrix-inversion method. The matrix-inversion approach reduces the problem to a two-dimensional matrix inversion, with all dynamical input encoded in two coefficients α and β that are rational functions of the coupling constants. The paper derives explicit formulae for the reflection and transmission coefficients and emphasizes that the only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter, namely the introduction of the imaginary part Y(x). The author illustrates the growing algebraic complexity of the determinant and numerator at increasing cutoff dimensions M = 2, 3, 4, noting that symbolic manipulation on a computer becomes necessary at M ≥ 4. The discussion situates the work within the broader PT-symmetry literature, highlighting the manifest asymmetry between in and out states, and concludes that the formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering is established, with the merit of the discrete model left for future study.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper develops a schematic, exactly solvable model of one-dimensional scattering in PT-symmetric quantum mechanics, where the potential V(x) is complex but possesses combined parity-time symmetry. The author begins by recalling the standard treatment of stationary one-dimensional motion via the ordinary differential Schrödinger equation, which admits either bound-state solutions with ψ(±∞) = 0 or scattering solutions with incoming and outgoing plane-wave boundary conditions. The conventional approach specifies reflection and transmission coefficients B and C once the normalization A = 1 is imposed. The recent generalization to non-Hermitian but quasi-Hermitian Hamiltonians, characterized by PT-symmetry, is then invoked, with the key review by Carl Bender cited as the source of this development. The present work focuses on a very simple PT-symmetric scattering model in which the potential is written as V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x), with Z even and real, and Y odd and real. Rather than solving the differential equation directly, the author replaces it with its Runge-Kutta-discretized, difference-equation representation, a purely numerical recipe whose accuracy improves as the lattice step h tends to zero. Assuming the potential vanishes beyond a cutoff distance, the discrete Schrödinger equation reduces to a tridiagonal linear system, which can be solved either by a matching method or by a matrix-inversion method. The matrix-inversion approach reduces the problem to a two-dimensional matrix inversion, with all dynamical input encoded in two coefficients α and β that are rational functions of the coupling constants. The paper derives explicit formulae for the reflection and transmission coefficients and emphasizes that the only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter, namely the introduction of the imaginary part Y(x). The author illustrates the growing algebraic complexity of the determinant and numerator at increasing cutoff dimensions M = 2, 3, 4, noting that symbolic manipulation on a computer becomes necessary at M ≥ 4. The discussion situates the work within the broader PT-symmetry literature, highlighting the manifest asymmetry between in and out states, and concludes that the formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering is established, with the merit of the discrete model left for future study.

Research Context
Standard quantum mechanics treats one-dimensional motion via the ordinary differential Schrödinger equation. The equation admits either bound-state or scattering regimes depending on the energy. Reflection and transmission coefficients are defined by imposing standard boundary conditions. The conventional approach has recently been generalized to non-Hermitian quasi-Hermitian Hamiltonians. PT-symmetry is the key idea behind this generalization, as summarized by Carl Bender. Few papers have addressed scattering in PT-symmetric systems, leaving a gap to fill.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper asks how scattering can be modeled in a PT-symmetric quantum system. The potential is hypothesized to be complex but PT-symmetric, with an even real part and odd imaginary part. The differential equation is hypothesized to be replaceable by its Runge-Kutta-discretized difference form. It is hypothesized that the reflection and transmission coefficients can be derived from this discretized equation. The main hypothesis is that the only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter. It is predicted that Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering share a formal parallelism. It is predicted that the problem remains tractable despite the in-out asymmetry.

Methodological Details
The study considers a one-dimensional scattering problem with a complex PT-symmetric short-range potential. The Schrödinger equation is discretized using a Runge-Kutta method. The discrete Schrödinger equation is −ψk−1 + (2 cos ϕ + Vk) ψk −ψk+1 = 0. The lattice points are defined as xk = k h with h > 0 and k = 0, ±1, ... The potential is assumed to vanish beyond a cutoff distance j = M, M+1, .... The energy variable ϕ is constrained by −2 ≤ 2 − h2E ≤ 2, i.e., E ∈ (0, 4/h2). The boundary conditions are discretized with A = 1, B, and C as reflection and transmission coefficients. The M = 1 model uses three nontrivial relations to derive B and C. The M = 2 model inserts four known quantities into a triplet of relations. The coupling constants are Z0, Z1, ..., ZM−1 and Y1, ..., YM−1. The matrix-inversion method reduces the problem to a two-dimensional matrix inversion. The inverse matrix R = T−1 has four corners that represent all dynamical input. The coefficients α and β are rational functions of the coupling constants. The determinant det T and numerator γ grow in complexity at higher dimensions. Symbolic manipulation on a computer is required at M ≥ 4.

Procedures And Architectures
The differential equation is discretized using the Runge-Kutta method. The lattice step h and cutoff 1/M are varied independently for quickest convergence. The two independent solutions in the vanishing-potential region are ρ± = exp(±iϕ). The matching method constructs solutions from the boundary conditions. The matching method yields C = 2i sin ϕ / (2i sin ϕ − Z0) and B = Z0 / (2i sin ϕ − Z0). The matrix-inversion method rewrites the equation as a doubly infinite system of linear algebraic equations. The system is reduced to a finite-dimensional tridiagonal non-square-matrix problem. The matrix T is partitioned to reveal redundant components. The inverse matrix R is partitioned into blocks α, β, and submatrices. The problem degenerates to two scalar relations for the amplitudes. The reflection and transmission coefficients are solved via elimination. The final formulae for B and C are given in terms of α and β. The determinant and numerator are computed explicitly for M = 2, 3, 4. The determinant for M = 2 is Z0Z1² − 2Z1 + Y1²2Z0. The determinant for M = 3 includes Y1²2Z0Z2² and other terms. The M = 4 case requires symbolic manipulation due to complexity. The coefficients α and β encode all dynamical input. The transmission and reflection coefficients have the same form in both cases.

Key Results
The reflection and transmission coefficients are derived from the discretized Schrödinger equation. The M = 1 model yields C = 2i sin ϕ / (2i sin ϕ − Z0). The M = 1 model yields B = Z0 / (2i sin ϕ − Z0). The M = 1 model remains Hermitian since no PT-symmetry has entered. The M = 2 model introduces the imaginary part Y−1. The M = 2 model yields det T = Z0Z1² − 2Z1 + Y1²2Z0. The M = 3 model yields det T with 15 products of couplings. The M = 4 model requires symbolic manipulation due to complexity. The coefficients α and β are rational functions of the coupling constants. The transmission and reflection coefficients have the same form in both cases. The dynamical input is encoded in the four corners of the inverse matrix R. The problem remains tractable by standard linear algebra techniques. The in-out asymmetry is shown to be merely formal. The only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter. No numerical values or datasets are reported.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering is established. The differences are represented by the differences in the form of the dynamical input. The dynamical input is encoded in the two functions α and β. The vanishing or non-vanishing coefficients Yk distinguish the two cases. The in-out asymmetry is a distinguishing feature of PT-symmetric scattering. The asymmetry is shown to be merely formal in the present model. The partitioning of the Schrödinger equation is key to the success. The reduction to two-dimensional matrix inversion simplifies the problem. The merits of the discrete model are not exhausted by the present analysis. Future study might illuminate the non-Hermitian inverse problem of scattering. The work fills a gap in the PT-symmetric scattering literature. The discrete model provides a schematic but exactly solvable framework.

Claims
The formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering is established. The transmission and reflection coefficients have the same form in both cases. The dynamical input is encoded in the two functions α and β. The differences are represented by the differences in the form of the dynamical input.  
The in-out asymmetry is shown to be merely formal in the present model.   
The only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter. The imaginary part Y(x) introduces the PT-symmetry.  The formal parallelism simplifies the study of PT-symmetric scattering.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering. 2. The strongest evidence is the derivation of the reflection and transmission coefficients. 3. The future path is the study of the non-Hermitian inverse problem of scattering.
